new_entities.name: Homeopathy meta-evidence
new_entities.description: The aggregate placebo-controlled evidence base for homeopathic interventions across clinical indications.

new_entities.name: Any outcome
new_entities.description: Any claimed clinical outcome across conditions rather than a disease-specific endpoint.

edges.effect_quant: A 1998 review of individualized homeopathy found an apparent pooled rate ratio of 1.62 versus placebo in 19 analyzable placebo-controlled trials, but the effect disappeared when analyses were restricted to the best trials; a 2017 meta-analysis of non-individualized homeopathy found pooled signals in lower-quality subsets but continued inconsistency once risk-of-bias filtering was applied.
edges.population: patients enrolled in placebo-controlled homeopathy trials across a wide range of conditions
edges.mechanism: Any observed benefit is difficult to separate from regression to the mean, contextual care effects, reporting bias, and weak or inconsistent trial methods, especially when higher-quality trials show attenuation toward null.
edges.summary: This is a claim-check edge about the overall evidence pattern, not a disease-specific endorsement. Homeopathy literature contains some positive pooled signals, but they are unstable, highly quality-sensitive, and not persuasive enough to treat homeopathy as a generally effective therapy across outcomes.
edges.caveats: Do not flatten this to 'all trials are identical' or 'all effects are zero.' The more careful reading is that headline-positive findings are common in weaker or selectively reported subsets, while the more reliable evidence base remains inconclusive or near-null.
